stimulus.text: "Why should Pennsylvania, founded by the English, become a Colony of Aliens, who will shortly be so numerous as to Germanize us instead of our Anglifying them, and will never adopt our Language or Customs, any more than they can acquire our Complexion." — Benjamin Franklin, "Observations Concerning the Increase of Mankind," 1751.
stimulus.source_note: Benjamin Franklin, "Observations Concerning the Increase of Mankind," 1751; public domain.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain primary source

primary_sources: Franklin, "Observations Concerning the Increase of Mankind" (1751)

stem: What does Franklin's complaint best show about German immigration to Pennsylvania?

options.text: That Germans were only a tiny minority in Pennsylvania at the time.
options.misconception: Franklin fears the Germans will soon be “so numerous” as to Germanize the colony; a tiny minority would not worry him.

options.text: That German immigrants were arriving in numbers large enough to worry English colonists.
That the Germans had already adopted the English language and customs completely.
options.misconception: Franklin complains of the opposite: the Germans “will never adopt our Language or Customs.”

options.text: That Franklin welcomed German immigration as a great strength for the colony.
options.misconception: Franklin is complaining, not welcoming; he fears Pennsylvania will become a colony of aliens.

rationales.general:
1. Hear the fear. Pennsylvania will be Germanized, not Anglified — the English becoming the minority.
2. Ask what makes that fear possible. Numbers: Germans arriving fast enough to outnumber the English.
3. Check the language complaint. They will never adopt English language or customs, Franklin says.
4. Name what the passage shows. Immigration on a scale large enough to alarm the English colonists.
Remember: Franklin's alarm is itself the evidence — Germans were coming in numbers big enough to scare an Englishman.
rationales.B: Franklin's fear only makes sense if German immigrants were arriving in large numbers: he worries they will “shortly be so numerous as to Germanize us instead of our Anglifying them.” A tiny minority could not Germanize a colony. Background: German and Scots-Irish immigration filled Pennsylvania in the early 1700s, many arriving as redemptioners who paid for passage after landing. The passage shows English colonists alarmed at the scale, not welcoming it.
rationales.A: Franklin fears the Germans will soon be “so numerous” as to Germanize the colony; a tiny minority would not worry him.
rationales.C: Franklin complains of the opposite: the Germans “will never adopt our Language or Customs.”
rationales.D: Franklin is complaining, not welcoming; he fears Pennsylvania will become a colony of aliens.
